newsitem.title: USA: China's dollar bonds steady in wake of Deng death.
newsitem.headline: China's dollar bonds steady in wake of Deng death.

text.p: China's dollar denominated sovereign debt barely budged on news that the country's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping died in Beijing earlier on Wednesday, traders and analysts said.
"The market is absorbing the news with great equanimity," said Joseph Taylor, vice president of sovereign debt research at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc.

Despite rampant speculation that Deng was gravely ill, China's 10-year global bond launched last year has hardly moved since last Friday. It was bid 72 basis points over U.S. Treasuries in afternoon action, firmer than the pricing of 110 basis points over Treasuries when it was launched.
China's 100-year issue was bid 135 basis points over 30 year Treasuries, compared to 299 basis points at its launch.
"There is a recognition that there has been a fair degree of tangible consolidation of political power over the last several years," Taylor said.
Bob Kapp, president of the U.S.-China Business Council, said U.S. companies doing business in China have long expected and prepared for the transition to a post-Deng era.
There is a strong prevailing belief that Deng's legacies of opening China to the outside world and his economic reforms are enduring, Kapp said.
"Whoever succeeds Deng works in a different world," he added. "There's no turning back."
While the fixed income market remained calm, some traders were bracing for stock turbulence early Thursday when markets open in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.
American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) of Chinese and Hong Kong issues traded in New York were unmoved by Deng's death.

But the Hong Kong Index comprising 30 major Hong Kong listed stocks traded on the American Stock Exchange, sold off mildly on the news. At 1515 EST/2015 GMT, the index was off 1.05 at 263.19 on light volume, according to an Amex official.

When stock trading opens Thursday in Hong Kong, "It is possible the Hang Seng index could drop 1.0 or 2.0 percent before recovering," said J.P. Wu, director of research at U.S. Securities and Futures.
John Roque, a technical analyst at Lehman Brothers, warned that the Hong Kong market was vulnerable if a mild selloff developed into heavy technical liquidation.
"The Hang Seng index has not made any progress since November," he said. "If the index dips below 12,700, it could head to 12,000."
On Wednesday, the Hang Seng closed at 13,106.32, up 3.38 points.
